name: Regulatory Dependency Mapping
description: Models a regulator's handbook as a graph: standards, the hierarchy of sections beneath them, and the cross-references sections make to one another. Answers which parts of a rulebook a proposed change reaches, which text is most expensive to change, and where one standard depends on another.

Standard.label: Standard
Standard.description: A named regulatory standard, handbook or sourcebook published by a supervisory authority — the highest level of the regulatory hierarchy. Sections hang beneath it.

id.description: Short identifier for the standard as the regulator publishes it, typically the sourcebook code. Expected to be the prefix from which section identifiers in this standard are built. e.g. `MIFIDPRU`.

Section.label: Section
Section.description: A single addressable unit of regulatory text — a chapter, section or subsection of a standard. Sections form the hierarchy of a handbook, cross-reference one another, and are the level at which regulatory change is tracked.

id.description: Section identifier exactly as the regulator cites it, including the standard prefix — a sourcebook code followed by chapter and section numbers. Expected to be unique across every standard, not merely within one. e.g. `COBS 4.2`.

title.description: Long heading of the section as published, conventionally repeating the section identifier before the heading text. e.g. `COBS 4.2 Reporting timetable`.

lastUpdated.description: Date on which the section's current text took effect in the handbook — the in-force date of the most recent amendment, not the date that amendment was announced or published. ISO 8601 zoned datetime; the time and zone carry no meaning beyond the calendar date, kept only because local imports require a zoned datetime rather than a bare date. This is the property regulatory-change analysis filters on. e.g. `2025-02-01T00:00:00Z`.

sectionInStandard.description: Places a top-level section directly beneath the standard that publishes it. Only sections at the top of a handbook's hierarchy carry this; deeper sections reach their standard through their parent section instead. A section sits directly beneath at most one standard, and carries either this or a DEPENDS_ON to a parent section, never both; a standard may have many top-level sections.

sectionInSection.description: Places a section beneath its immediate parent section in the handbook hierarchy, read child to parent. Chaining these from a top-level section reconstructs the full depth of a handbook. A section has at most one parent section, and carries either this or a DEPENDS_ON to a standard, never both; a section may have many child sections, or none.

sectionRelated.description: Records a cross-reference made by the citing (from) section to the cited (to) section, so that a change to the cited text is known to reach the citing text. Direction is the direction of the citation, not of influence; two sections that cite each other carry one of these each way. A section may cite many others, or none, and be cited by many, or by none.

subsection.description: The specific rule within the cited (to) section that the citing section refers to, in the regulator's own rule notation. Where a section is cited as a whole this is expected to be the cited section's own identifier. e.g. `COBS 3.1.1.5R`.
